The length-based onset of puberty in this species is considerably later than in smaller-bodied lutjanid congeners, a pattern that reflects the trade-off between delayed reproduction and the attainment of a body size that enhances both competitive ability on the reef and fecundity per spawning event.

Longevity records for Chinamanfish indicate a maximum lifespan of 37 years [am = 37 years] under ambient thermal conditions of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], a duration that places this species among the longer-lived members of the family Lutjanidae. This extended life span is consistent with a life-history strategy characterised by slow somatic growth, delayed sexual maturation, and iteroparous reproduction over multiple decades. Otolith-based age validation studies have confirmed that individuals can persist well beyond thirty years in undisturbed habitats, with the oldest documented specimen exhibiting 37 annually deposited growth increments. Such longevity, coupled with the species' moderate body size, suggests a relatively low natural mortality rate once individuals have recruited to the adult reef-associated population.

The overall life-history profile of Symphorus nematophorus combines moderate adult body size with extreme longevity, a combination that places it at the slower end of the fast-slow continuum among Indo-Pacific reef fishes.
